But perhaps love would find her decidedly unattractive after all, whispered the voices; there was a reason, they said, why the truth was kept hidden for so long.
"That was cowardice," said the optician, shifting his leather bag to the other hip, as the jostling of the bag and voices began to cause a slow discomfort.
"That was prudence," the voices said, "Fear is sometimes a good advisor," they added while humming the theme melody of the early evening series.
The optician now slowed down.
The walk to Selma's house, which usually took ten minutes, suddenly felt like a day's journey; a day's journey with lots and lots of baggage.

The dog was the color of slushy snow, a washed-out grey and shaggy like a purebred Irish Wolfhound with nothing else mixed in.
His body was still small, but his paws were as large as bear paws, and we all knew what that meant.
Selma was still standing upright in front of the kitchen bench.
She looked at the dog for a long time.
Then she looked at my father as if he were a gift idea store.
Farmer Häubel was firmly convinced that death would be polite, just as Farmer Häubel himself had been his entire life.
He was certain that death would not wrench life from him, but gently take it from his hand.
He imagined Death knocking politely, opening the door just a crack and asking "May I come in?" to which Farmer Häubel would naturally say yes.
"Of course," Farmer Häubel would say, "do come in," and Death would enter.
He would stand by Farmer Häubel's bed and ask: "Is this a good time for you?"
"I can also come by at a later time. "
Farmer Häubel would straighten up and say, "No, no, it suits me very well right now,"
"Let's not postpone it again, who knows when you will be able to arrange it next time," and death would sit down on the already prepared chair at the head of the table.
He would apologize in advance for the coldness of his hands, which he knew wouldn't bother Farmer Häubel at all, and then he would place a hand on Farmer Häubel's eyes.
The people in the village were anxious, it was evident, even though most of them tried not to show it.
This morning, just a few hours after Selma's dream, people in the village were moving as if black ice had formed on every path.
Not only outdoors but also in the houses black ice in the kitchens and living rooms.
They moved as if their own bodies were completely foreign to them, as if all their joints were inflamed and even the objects they handled were highly inflammable.
All day long they suspected their own life and, as much as possible, the lives of everyone else.

Again and again they looked behind them to check if someone was charging at them with murderous intent, someone who had lost their mind and therefore had nothing of note left to lose, and they quickly looked forward again because after all, a mindless person could also attack from the front.
They looked up to rule out falling roof tiles, branches or heavy lampshades.
They avoided all animals, as they believed the outbreak could occur faster in them than in humans.
They circled around the good-natured cows, who might be frisky today; they avoided dogs, even very old ones barely able to stand but who might still make a go for one's throat today.
On such days anything was possible; even decrepit dachshunds could bite your throat after all, it wasn't much more far-fetched than an okapi.
Except for Selma's sister-in-law Elsbeth, the villagers were mostly not superstitious.
They did carelessly all the things that one should not do out of superstition.

They sat calmly under wall clocks, even though superstition holds that to do so can bring death; they slept with their heads towards the door, even though according to superstition, this would mean being carried out feet first through the very same door.
They hung laundry between Christmas and New Year, which, as Elsbeth warned, in superstition is equivalent to a suicide or aiding and abetting a murder.
They weren't scared when the owl called at night, when a horse in the stable was sweating heavily, when a dog was howling at night with its head bowed low.
The train ride lasted fifteen minutes, with no stops in between.
Since our first train ride, we always played the same game:
We would stand with our backs to the windows by the opposite train doors, Martin would close his eyes, and I would look out of the train door window that was behind Martin.
In first class, I pointed out to Martin everything I saw during the journey, and Martin tried to memorize it all.

This worked out very well, so that by the second year of school I no longer had to dictate anything, and Martin, with his back to the window and his eyes closed, could recite almost everything I saw through the steamed-up train window: "Wire factory," he said exactly at the moment we passed by the wire factory.

She put a slice of cheese on the bread, folded it over, and placed it in my sandwich box.
"Do you know exactly when you had this dream?"
"About three o'clock," said Selma.
She was startled awake after the vision of the Okapi faded.
Sitting upright in bed, she looked down at her nightgown in which she had been standing on the Uhlheck in her dream and then glanced at the alarm clock.
Three o'clock.
"We probably shouldn't take this so seriously," said Selma, but she said it as a television detective who doesn't take an anonymous letter too seriously.
"What's the matter?"
I asked.
"Nothing," Selma chirped, opening the refrigerator, pulling out a pack of sliced cheese and liver sausage, and waving them through the air.
"Little mouse," she cooed after him, and the cooing and 'little mouse' were indeed alarming.
"Cheese, please," I said, "what do you have?"
"Nothing," trilled Selma, "I did say that.
She spread butter onto a slice of bread, and because she was still slacking off, she knocked the cheese off the counter with her wrist.
Selma now stood still, looking down at the package of cheese as though it were something precious that had shattered into a thousand pieces.
Selma had dreamed of an okapi three times in her life, and after each time someone had died.
Therefore, we were convinced that the dream of an Okapi and death were certainly connected.
That's how our mind works.
He can ensure in the shortest time that the most divergent things firmly belong together.
Coffee pots and shoelaces, for example, or deposit bottles and fir trees.
When I slept downstairs with Selma, she would tell me bedtime stories with happy endings.
When I was younger, after the stories, I would always hold her wrist, put my thumb on her pulse and imagine that the whole world did everything to the rhythm of Selma's heartbeat.

I imagined the optician grinding lenses, Martin lifting a weight, Elsbeth trimming her hedge, the retailer stocking juice boxes, my mother layering fir branches, my father stamping prescriptions, and they all did this precisely to Selma's heartbeat rhythm.
I had always reliably fallen asleep to this, but now, at ten years old, Selma thought I was too old for that.
